title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Reach the Peak, but Choosing the Next Mountain Still Takes a Human
dek: Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local optimum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still depends on human intuition.
why: A structural judgment from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest opportunity in consumer AI is joy, not efficiency. The views are often counterintuitive, good for stress-testing your own product roadmap.
who: Founders and product leads who are using AI to change their own products or restructure company processes, and investors interested in AI's impact on jobs and consumer opportunities.
skip: If you're short on time, you can skip the final book list, life mottos, and DJ anecdotes without losing the AI judgment.

points.h: The AI era will not replicate winner-take-all
points.body: The AI era will not produce winner-take-all the way mobile internet did: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, but in the AI stack each layer now has about 20 relevant participants. Two years ago everyone thought coding agents would end up with a single winner, yet today Claude Code, Codex, Lovable, and Replit are all moving forward at once. Anish says the people at the frontier in labs believe what's actually happening is autocatalytic effects—using new technology to improve your own processes—rather than recursive self-improvement, so there won't be a runaway winner that swallows everyone. The takeaway for founders: don't bet on a single full-stack giant; every layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has long-term room.

points.h: CEOs want to build bigger companies, not fewer employees
points.body: Employees probably don't need to worry too much about being replaced by AI, not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because CEOs are incentivized by growth, not shrinking. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion company. A Google executive friend told Anish that the company isn't laying people off but using AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and now the hard problem is "what to add to the roadmap." When execution is no longer scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things for a bigger goal.

points.h: Companies will become loops, and the next step needs a human decision
points.body: The company form is shifting from a list of roles and departments to a cascade of loops: first automation of individual workflows, then functional loops, then cross-departmental, and eventually loops running most of the company's operations. The loops themselves keep producing output, and that output becomes input for the next layer of loops; some mechanism sends signals back to the CEO—when to adjust the business entity, when to change strategy. This mechanism can help a company climb to a local maximum, but after the plateau it must rely on human intuition for out-of-distribution thinking to place the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Asking AI to directly come up with a million-dollar idea often fails, because humans can set the direction right, while AI is only responsible for sweeping along a given slope.

points.h: Users want to spend time, not save it
points.body: Silicon Valley defaults to AI's value being efficiency, but Anish thinks that's a misjudgment: most people don't really want to save time; they want to spend it where it brings connection, love, progress, and fun. The biggest products in history have always been entertainment and social, so AI's consumer opportunity is not "a few more minutes saved" but making loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, more progress, or more fun. He criticizes that for the past 40 years technology has been extending intelligence and hardly extending the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

points.h: AI is decoupling skill from desire
points.body: Anish sees AI not just as a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface—it can separate "skill" from "desire." People who want to make music are no longer blocked by "can't play piano"; people who want to write code don't have to first learn enough to hold a job; personal identity is thus amplified. He recalls that the high-risk environment of the 1950s-60s greatly stimulated human potential, and thinks the current world is in a low-risk state, and AI has a chance to pull GDP growth from 2% to 10-15%—provided it raises not the speed of a single link but the scale of what a group dares to imagine.

points.h: Ideas that are too small now can't get funding
points.body: Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was too much; today at a16z, the reverse standard has arrived—if an idea can still only be that small with AI's help, they simply won't invest. "Unbounded ambition" has become the core value for screening companies; Marc Andreessen's phrasing is: we either go to the moon or leave a moon-sized crater.

points.h: Shipping something small every week is how you build product intuition
points.body: The most direct advice for product people is the old line: build more things. Find a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a "chassis," run each new model through it, ship the finished product, discuss it with people—that's the path to building AI intuition. The cadence only needs to be one small release per week; going crazy isn't sustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and photos, auto-scoring, and finally generating 20 pages reviewing their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. It's small, but this kind of work lets you repeatedly taste AI's "moments of joy"—once you taste it, you can't go back.
